title: SR&ED Deduction Against Income - Canadian Tax Glossary
description: Discover how the SR&ED Deduction Against Income reduces your corporate taxable income in our Canadian R&D tax credit glossary.
summary: The SR&ED deduction against income lets taxpayers carrying on business in Canada pool eligible current and, after December 15, 2024, capital SR&ED expenditures under section 37 of the Income Tax Act and deduct them from business income. Corporations may defer the pool indefinitely, but federal ITCs claimed and government assistance reduce it, and negative balances become taxable income.

body.text: The SR&ED deduction against income lets taxpayers carrying on business in Canada pool eligible current and, after December 15, 2024, capital SR&ED expenditures under section 37 of the Income Tax Act and deduct them from business income. Corporations may defer the pool indefinitely, but federal ITCs claimed and government assistance reduce it, and negative balances become taxable income.

As of November 2026, Canada's Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program—projected in Department of Finance Budget 2026 tax-expenditure tables at $4.7 billion to $5.5 billion annually (rising toward $6.4 billion over the fiscal horizon) and supporting 20,000 to 24,000 claimant businesses per year according to tax-practice analyses—operates under its largest statutory expansion in over a decade. Under Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026 and applies retroactively to taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, Parliament doubled the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% refundable investment tax credit (ITC) from $3 million to $6 million (increasing maximum annual federal cash refunds on current expenditures from $1.05 million to $2.1 million), widened the prior-year taxable capital phase-out range from $10 million–$50 million to $15 million–$75 million, extended the enhanced 35% refundable credit to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) via a three-year average gross revenue test (which Canadian-controlled private corporations [CCPCs] may also elect to use), and restored SR&ED deductions and ITCs for depreciable capital property acquired and equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024. Operationally, the CRA launched an optional upfront pre-claim approval process on April 1, 2026 that issues technical eligibility determinations within eight weeks. Subsequently, on November 5, 2026, Federal Budget 2026 (Masters of Our Destiny) proposed an additional $930 million five-year SR&ED expansion—requiring Parliamentary enactment for taxation years beginning on or after November 5, 2026—to cover initial regulatory certification testing and intellectual property (IP) registration and maintenance expenses, while again omitting a federal Patent Box regime. Across the provinces, British Columbia permanently enacted full alignment with the federal $6 million limit and ECPC rules in 2026, Québec abolished seven legacy R&D tax credits in favour of its refundable Tax Credit for R&D and Pre-Commercialization (CRIC) alongside its 2% Incentive Deduction for the Commercialization of Innovations (IDCI) IP Box, and jurisdictions such as Ontario and Alberta retained independent expenditure caps and capital rules.
1. Executive Legislative Landscape and the 2024–2026 Reform Cycle
1.1 Evolution from the 2024 Fall Economic Statement to Bill C-15 Enactment

Between December 2024 and March 2026, Canadian federal R&D tax law underwent a multi-stage legislative overhaul that reversed major restrictions enacted in Federal Budget 2012 (which had eliminated capital expenditures after 2013 and trimmed proxy overhead and subcontractor inclusion rates). Tax auditors and corporate claimants reviewing taxation years spanning 2024, 2025, and 2026 must distinguish rigorously between superseded consultation thresholds and the final statutory text enacted into the Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.) (ITA).

On December 16, 2024, the Government of Canada tabled the 2024 Fall Economic Statement, announcing plans to expand the SR&ED program effective for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024 (codified statutorily as taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024) and for depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024. On August 15, 2025, the Department of Finance released draft legislative proposals for public consultation, with stakeholder submissions closing on September 12, 2025. Under both the December 2024 statement and the August 2025 draft legislative package, the enhanced 35% ITC annual expenditure limit was initially proposed to increase from $3 million to $4.5 million, corresponding to a maximum annual refundable credit of $1.575 million.

When the Minister of Finance and National Revenue, the Honourable François-Philippe Champagne, tabled Budget 2025 on November 4, 2025, the federal government superseded the interim $4.5 million consultation figure and raised the enhanced 35% annual SR&ED expenditure limit further to $6 million, preserving the retroactive effective date for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024. Parliament incorporated these amendments into Bill C-15 (An Act to implement certain provisions of the budget tabled in Parliament on November 4, 2025, short-titled the Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1). Amended Bill C-15 passed third reading in the House of Commons on February 26, 2026—the date of substantive enactment for Canadian financial-statement tax provisioning—and received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026. Accordingly, any secondary commentary citing a $4.5 million federal expenditure limit or a $1.575 million maximum federal refund reflects superseded pre-November 2025 proposals rather than enacted law. Industry data citing CRA fiscal year 2024–2025 statistics underscores the breadth of firms affected by these reforms: out of roughly $4.5 billion in allowed ITCs prior to the expansion, 64% of claims originated from small businesses with under $4 million in revenue, led sectorally by Software and Information Technology at 40.8% ($1.84 billion), Electrical Engineering at 13.6% ($612 million), Medical Science at 13.1% ($590 million), Mechanical Engineering at 12.8% ($576 million), Chemistry and Chemical Engineering at 6.8% ($306 million), and Other Fields at 12.9% ($581 million).
1.2 Budget 2026 Proposed Commercialization and Intellectual Property Expansion

On November 5, 2026, Minister Champagne tabled Budget 2026 – Masters of Our Destiny in the House of Commons. Leaving statutory personal and corporate income tax rates unchanged, Budget 2026 proposed a $930 million five-year expansion of the SR&ED program ($25 million in 2026–27, $200 million in 2027–28, $245 million in 2028–29, $225 million in 2029–30, and $235 million in 2030–31) targeting commercialization and domestic IP retention. Unlike the enacted Bill C-15 reforms, the Budget 2026 SR&ED announcements remain un-enacted legislative proposals as of November 15, 2026; once passed by Parliament, they will apply to taxation years that begin on or after November 5, 2026 (Budget Day).

First, under the proposed Regulatory and Certification Requirements expansion, eligible SR&ED activities would broaden to include tests, technological validations, and studies carried out to satisfy regulatory requirements for obtaining the initial approval or certification needed to commercialize a product or process. To qualify, such validation work must relate directly to a project that is eligible under existing SR&ED rules, and claimants would claim the same expenditure categories (wages and salaries, materials, contracting costs, overhead, and machinery and equipment) applicable to core SR&ED.

Second, under the proposed Intellectual Property Protection expansion, qualified SR&ED expenditures would include expenses reasonably incurred to prepare, file, obtain, and periodically maintain legal protection for IP developed in the course of conducting an eligible SR&ED project. Qualifying IP is restricted strictly to patents, certificates of supplementary protection, plant breeders' rights, and copyrighted software registered or protected under relevant Canadian legislation or equivalent foreign statutes. Trademarks are excluded, as are expenses to enforce IP rights (such as patent infringement litigation) or costs not directly connected to securing and maintaining IP protection. Under a specialized territorial rule, official administrative fees paid to foreign patent or IP offices outside Canada would be eligible, whereas supporting professional activities—such as patent application drafting and prosecution preparation—would qualify only if conducted in Canada. If a taxpayer later disposes of IP for which SR&ED IP-protection incentives were claimed, recapture rules will claw back the associated SR&ED deductions and ITCs.
1.3 Status of the Federal Patent Box Consultation vs. Cost-Based Super-Deductions

A defining feature of Canada's innovation tax landscape as of late 2026 is the continued absence of a federal Patent Box. Although the Department of Finance conducted formal consultations on a federal Patent Box regime in early 2024 and the 2024 Fall Economic Statement (as well as the governing party's 2025 election platform) promised an IP-income tax preference, both Budget 2025 and Budget 2026 omitted a federal Patent Box. No bill, Canada Gazette notice, or draft legislative proposal creating a preferential federal tax rate on IP-derived income has been released through November 2026, leaving Québec's IDCI as the sole subnational IP Box operating in Canada.

Rather than enacting an income-based Patent Box, the federal government has relied on accelerated capital cost allowance (CCA) super-deductions, direct IP grant funding, and targeted capital gains exemptions. Under Bill C-15 (Royal Assent March 26, 2026), Parliament enacted the Productivity Super-Deduction, reinstating the Accelerated Investment Incentive for property acquired after 2024, restoring immediate write-offs for manufacturing and processing machinery and equipment, clean energy generation and conservation equipment, and zero-emission vehicles, and providing immediate expensing for productivity-enhancing assets—including acquired patents, data network infrastructure, and computers—acquired on or after April 16, 2024 and becoming available for use before January 1, 2027. On September 15, 2026 (followed by draft legislative and regulatory proposals on October 1, 2026, reaffirmed in Budget 2026), the government unveiled the proposed Productivity Mega Deduction, expanding 100% immediate expensing to more than 65% of business capital assets acquired on or after September 15, 2026, including patents, software, fibre-optic cables and data network infrastructure, mining property and equipment, oil and gas pipelines, vehicles, and roads, while raising the deduction for Canadian development expenses (CDE) from a 30% declining-balance rate to 100%. Because CCA measures accelerate tax depreciation on the cost of acquiring capital assets rather than reducing the corporate tax rate on ongoing licensing or embedded IP profits, policy analysts note they do not substitute for a Patent Box on internally generated IP.

Alongside these CCA measures, Budget 2026 extended Canada's Clean Economy ITCs (such as the Clean Technology ITC and Clean Technology Manufacturing ITC at up to 30% and the Electric Vehicle Supply Chain ITC at 10%) to 2040, extended the Mineral Exploration Tax Credit (METC) and Critical Mineral Exploration Tax Credit (CMETC, adding antimony) to March 31, 2032, and proposed the Canada Growth Incentive (CGI)—a capital gains exemption of up to $15 million per qualifying business for Canadian-resident individuals selling qualifying corporation shares issued on or after November 5, 2026 and before 2037. Budget 2026 also allocated $75 million over three years (starting 2026–27) to extend the National Research Council's (NRC) IP Assist program, $22.5 million over three years (starting 2026–27) for the Innovation Asset Collective's Patent Collective, and $58 million over four years (starting 2027–28) for the Courts Administration Service to bolster Federal Court IP adjudication, while proposing Patent Act amendments requiring patent ownership changes to be registered with the Canadian Intellectual Property Office (CIPO), minimum statutory standards for patent infringement demand letters, and a broader Federal Intellectual Property Review with further measures anticipated in spring 2027.

body.text: 2. Statutory Architecture of the Federal SR&ED Program

Canada's federal SR&ED program delivers two distinct statutory tax incentives under the Income Tax Act and Part XXIX of the Income Tax Regulations. First, section 37 of the ITA permits taxpayers carrying on a business in Canada to pool allowable current and (post-December 15, 2024) capital SR&ED expenditures, deducting them in computing business income in the current year or carrying undeducted pool balances forward indefinitely. Second, sections 127 and 127.1 of the ITA provide refundable and/or non-refundable Investment Tax Credits (ITCs) at 35% or 15% on "qualified expenditures".
2.1 Definition of Qualifying SR&ED Work Under Subsection 248(1)

Every federal SR&ED claim—as well as subnational R&D claims across Canada—rests on the statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" in subsection 248(1) of the ITA, which conforms generally to the OECD Frascati Manual. Subsection 248(1) defines SR&ED as a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis" falling within three primary research categories—(a) basic research (undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view), (b) applied research (undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view), or (c) experimental development (undertaken to achieve technological advancement for creating new, or incrementally improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes)—together with commensurate supporting work directly in support of those activities in Canada, restricted specifically to engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research.

Under CRA administrative doctrine (Guidelines on the Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Tax Incentives, restructured in August 2021 around the "Why" and "How" of R&D), an eligible SR&ED project consists of interrelated activities conducted by qualified individuals necessary to resolve scientific or technological uncertainty—a capability gap or system-level unpredictability that cannot be resolved through standard practice or publicly available knowledge—in pursuit of a scientific or technological advancement. Achieving commercial novelty, uniqueness, feature enhancements, or expanded software functionality does not by itself establish technological advancement. Moreover, SR&ED eligibility terminates immediately on the project completion date: the moment the technological advancement is achieved by resolving the uncertainty, the uncertainty is determined to be unresolvable, or the project is terminated. Work in the social sciences or humanities, routine quality control, market research, and commercial production are statutorily excluded, and software modernization or scale-up using established methodologies does not qualify.
2.2 The Section 37 Deductible SR&ED Expenditure Pool and Carryforward Rules

Subsection 37(1) establishes a cumulative running account—the pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures—for taxpayers carrying on business in Canada. Deductions from the pool are optional in any given year (except for partnerships), enabling corporations to defer section 37 deductions indefinitely to shelter future taxable income rather than creating time-limited non-capital losses.

Increases to the subsection 37(1) pool encompass in-house current expenditures on SR&ED carried on in Canada under paragraph 37(1)(a) and subsection 37(8) (directly engaged salaries and wages, materials consumed or transformed, post-December 15, 2024 ASA equipment lease costs, and—solely under the traditional method per clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A) and Regulation 2900(2)–(3)—overhead and other expenditures); permissible foreign SR&ED employee wages up to 10% of Canadian SR&ED wages under subsection 37(1.4); 100% of current contract expenditures performed in Canada on the claimant's behalf under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01); 100% of qualifying third-party payments to Canadian corporations under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.1) or to approved associations, universities, colleges, research institutes, paragraph 149(1)(j) tax-exempt non-profit SR&ED corporations, and granting organizations under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(ii) clauses (A), (B), (C), and (E) (clause (D) having been repealed in 1996); and, following Bill C-15, restored capital expenditures under paragraph 37(1)(b) and subsection 37(8) for new or used depreciable property acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024 meeting the ≥90% SR&ED operating-time or value-consumption test. (Current expenditures for R&ED contract work performed outside Canada cannot enter the section 37 pool or earn ITCs, though they remain deductible in computing ordinary business income or loss under general tax principles.)

Decreases to the subsection 37(1) pool under paragraphs 37(1)(d) to (h) include all government assistance and non-government assistance (including provincial R&D tax credits and direct grants) received, entitled to be received, or reasonably expected to be received (paragraph 37(1)(d)), federal SR&ED ITCs claimed (applied against tax or refunded) in the preceding taxation year, prior-year pool deductions, and prior-year insolvency deductions. Whenever pool reductions exceed pool additions—creating a negative pool balance at year-end (for instance, where prior-year ITCs generated via the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount exceed current-year pool additions)—the negative amount is included in taxable income for the year, resetting the pool to zero. Under subsection 37(8) and CRA policy, no deduction or ITC is permitted for expenditures to acquire rights in, or arising out of, SR&ED, preventing duplicate claims between an R&D performer and an IP buyer.
2.3 Section 127 and Section 127.1 Investment Tax Credits and Refundability Mechanics

While section 37 governs income deductions, subsection 127(9) defines "qualified expenditure" and "investment tax credit" for credit computation, and section 127.1 (subsections 127.1(2) and 127.1(2.01)) governs "refundable investment tax credits", deeming refundable credits to be payments on account of tax that yield direct cash disbursements where credits exceed federal tax liability. Taxpayers hold statutory discretion over whether and in what order to deduct non-refundable ITCs (Ainsworth Lumber).

Auditors must verify four structural divergences between the section 37 deductible pool and subsection 127(9) qualified expenditures: (1) the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) enters qualified expenditures for ITC calculation (Form T661, Line 502) but never enters the section 37 deductible pool; (2) arm's-length Canadian SR&ED contracts and third-party payments enter the section 37 pool at 100% but enter qualified expenditures for ITCs at 80% (Line 529); (3) used depreciable equipment acquired after December 15, 2024 enters the section 37 pool at 100% (Line 390) if meeting the ≥90% SR&ED test, but earns 0% SR&ED ITC; and (4) Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) acquired after December 15, 2024 (>50% SR&ED operating time) never enters the section 37 pool (being depreciated via ordinary CCA on Schedule 8), but earns SR&ED ITCs on 25% of capital cost per period up to 50% total (Line 504).
2.4 Special Structural Rules for Partnerships, Corporate Control, and Loss Restriction Events
Corporate restructurings, joint ventures, and venture-capital financings trigger three high-stakes statutory rules in the ITA:

First, partnerships (subsections 37(1), 96(1), 127(8), 127(13), and 127(30)–(31)) face severe structural disadvantages compared to corporations or unincorporated joint ventures. Because a partnership is not a taxpayer (subsection 248(1)), it cannot carry forward any balance in its section 37 SR&ED pool; the entire pool must be deducted in calculating partnership net income or loss in the current fiscal period. Any resulting partnership loss attributable to SR&ED deductions is disallowed completely to limited partners and "specified members" (subsection 248(1)—passive partners not regularly, continuously, and substantially active in the partnership's business or a similar business during the year): the disallowed loss cannot be transferred to general partners, does not become a limited partnership loss or non-capital loss, and leaves the partner's adjusted cost base unchanged. Under subsection 127(8), partnerships earn SR&ED ITCs solely at the 15% basic rate, cannot allocate ITCs to specified members, and even where a general partner is a qualifying CCPC, the allocated 15% partnership ITC is 0% refundable (All Colour Chemicals). Furthermore, a partner cannot be an employee of the partnership—meaning any "salary" paid to a partner is treated as a profit distribution and is ineligible as SR&ED wages—and partnerships are barred from non-arm's-length expenditure transfers under subsection 127(13) (while excess ITC recapture flows through tiered partnerships under subsection 127(31) and paragraph 37(1)(c.3)). Conversely, participants in a contractual joint venture file independent SR&ED claims for their own expenditures, preserving 35% CCPC refundability.

Second, corporate control (sections 251 and 256) governs eligibility for both CCPC and ECPC enhanced 35% refundable credits. Losing CCPC or ECPC status—dropping the federal credit from a 35% cash refund to a 15% non-refundable carryforward—can occur not only through majority voting share transfers (de jure control) but also through shareholder agreements or options granting non-residents a contingent right to acquire control, or through factual (de facto) control where a non-resident or non-qualifying public entity exercises dominant operational or financial influence (HSC Research, Mimetex Pharmaceutical, Mindready Solutions, Aeronautic Development Corp., CO2 Solution Technologies).

Third, loss restriction events (section 37)—such as an acquisition of control of a corporation or trust—restrict the carryforward of undeducted section 37 SR&ED pool balances and unused non-refundable ITCs. Following a loss restriction event, pre-closing SR&ED pool balances may be deducted only if the specific business to which the SR&ED related continues to be carried on for profit or with a reasonable expectation of profit, and only against income from that same business or a substantially similar business.
3. Federal Tax Credit Rates, Expenditure Thresholds, and Phase-Out Formulas
3.1 Enhanced 35% vs. Basic 15% Investment Tax Credit Tiers
Under enacted Bill C-15, federal SR&ED ITCs follow a two-tier structure for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024:

The enhanced 35% ITC (subsection 127(10.1)) applies to qualifying CCPCs and Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) on qualified SR&ED expenditures up to their annual $6,000,000 expenditure limit (doubled from $3,000,000 prior to December 16, 2024). For current expenditures, the 35% ITC is 100% refundable, delivering up to $2,100,000 per year in cash even where the claimant has zero revenue or tax payable. For restored capital expenditures (new depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024), the 35% ITC is 40% refundable.

The basic 15% ITC (subsection 127(9)) applies to qualified expenditures of CCPCs and ECPCs exceeding their annual expenditure limit, as well as to all qualified expenditures of foreign-controlled Canadian subsidiaries, non-qualifying public corporations, Canadian branches of non-resident corporations, partnerships, and individuals and trusts. For foreign-controlled and non-qualifying public corporations (and for ECPCs above their expenditure limit), the 15% ITC is 0% refundable. For individuals and trusts, 40% of the 15% ITC is refundable. For qualifying CCPCs spending above their expenditure limit, 40% of the 15% excess ITC is refundable unless prior-year associated taxable income exceeded $500,000 or prior-year associated taxable capital exceeded $75,000,000.
3.2 Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) and Qualifying CCPCs

To prevent Canadian scale-up companies from forfeiting 35% refundable SR&ED credits upon listing publicly in Canada, Bill C-15 created the Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC) category for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024. To qualify as an ECPC, a corporation must satisfy all three statutory conditions throughout the taxation year:

items: Have a class of shares listed on a designated stock exchange (or have elected, or been designated by the Minister of National Revenue, to be a public corporation).
Not be controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever, by one or more non-resident persons.

body.text: In addition, Canadian-resident corporate subsidiaries in which all or substantially all (≥90%) of the shares are owned by one or more ECPCs are also eligible to access the enhanced 35% refundable credit, sharing the corporate group's expenditure limit.
3.3 Dual Phase-Out Mechanics: Taxable Capital vs. Three-Year Average Gross Revenue Election
Bill C-15 broadened the phase-out corridor for the $6,000,000 expenditure limit from $10,000,000–$50,000,000 to $15,000,000–$75,000,000 and introduced two alternative phase-out structures.

Under the Taxable Capital Structure (default for CCPCs), the $6,000,000 limit begins phasing out on a straight-line basis once the associated corporate group's prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada exceeds $15,000,000, reaching $0 at $75,000,000. Associated CCPCs allocate the shared expenditure limit across group members on T2 Schedule 49.

Under the Gross Revenue Structure (mandatory for ECPCs; elective for CCPCs), the $6,000,000 limit phases out on a straight-line basis once average annual gross revenue over the three preceding taxation years exceeds $15,000,000, reaching $0 at $75,000,000. For corporate groups preparing consolidated financial statements, gross revenue is the consolidated revenue reported in annual financial statements presented to shareholders at the highest level of consolidation, and group members share a single expenditure limit; for standalone corporations, gross revenue is GAAP annual financial-statement revenue presented to shareholders.

Crucially, each CCPC has the statutory option to elect the three-year average gross revenue structure instead of the taxable capital structure whenever doing so produces a larger expenditure limit. Consequently, capital-heavy biotechnology, clean-tech, semiconductor, or hardware CCPCs carrying more than $15 million—or even more than $75 million—in equity/debt capital on their balance sheets while generating under $15 million in three-year average revenue can elect the gross revenue method and retain the entire $6,000,000 expenditure limit ($2,100,000 cash refund). Across the $60,000,000 straight-line corridor ($15,000,000 to $75,000,000), the enacted expenditure limit (before short-year proration) equals $6,000,000 × Max(0, $75,000,000 − Phase-Out Metric) ÷ $60,000,000, reducing the $6,000,000 limit by $0.10 for every $1.00 of prior-year taxable capital or three-year average gross revenue above $15,000,000. (Under the August 2025 draft proposals when the proposed base limit was $4,500,000 over the same $60,000,000 range, the straight-line reduction rate was $0.075 per $1.00; raising the base limit to $6,000,000 in Budget 2025 / Bill C-15 increased the linear reduction slope to $0.10 per $1.00 across the identical $15M–$75M corridor.)
3.4 Carrybacks, Carryforwards, and Next-Year Taxability of Investment Tax Credits

Unused non-refundable federal SR&ED ITCs may be carried back 3 taxation years to offset prior Part I federal tax paid and carried forward up to 20 taxation years. Federal SR&ED ITCs—whether refunded in cash or applied to reduce federal tax—are taxable in the following taxation year by reducing the subsection 37(1) SR&ED deductible pool in that subsequent year (or generating an immediate income inclusion if the pool becomes negative). By contrast, provincial R&D tax credits constitute government assistance that reduces the federal SR&ED pool and qualified expenditure base in the current taxation year.

body.text: 4. Qualifying Expenditures (QREs) and Calculation Methodologies
4.1 Salaries and Wages, Specified Employees, Permissible Foreign Work, and Unpaid Remuneration

Employment salaries and wages (subsection 248(1)) paid for SR&ED carried on in Canada constitute the backbone of most claims (roughly 64% of claimed expenses according to industry summaries) and generate the largest tax credit multiplier under the proxy overhead method. Under both the proxy and traditional methods, only the portion of salary or wages of employees directly engaged in SR&ED—"hands-on" experimentation, technical analysis, direct technical supervision, and commensurate support work—qualifies as direct SR&ED labour, determined strictly by actual tasks performed rather than job titles. While claimants must substantiate time allocations with reliable project tracking (Synchrosat, Ergorecherche, Tuna Temple), the Tax Court held in AG Shield Canada Ltd. v. The Queen (2017 TCC 68) that where a shareholder-engineer's employment compensation was specifically structured to remunerate solely SR&ED work (leaving non-SR&ED executive duties unremunerated or compensated via dividends), the CRA could not arbitrarily prorate those SR&ED wages down by time spent on other corporate duties. Similarly, Oldcastle (2016 TCC 183) confirmed that remuneration meeting the subsection 248(1) definition of salary or wages was not disqualified as sales commission.

Several statutory exclusions and caps govern SR&ED payroll audits. Under subsection 37(8) and subsection 78(4), employee remuneration not actually paid within 180 days after the end of the taxation year is deemed not incurred in that year (nor are contingent wages payable only if SR&ED is approved; Jaft, 2015 MBCA 77), non-cash taxable benefits and stock option benefits (excluded for post-November 14, 2005 years, overriding Alcatel) are ineligible, retiring allowances are barred under the proxy method, partner draws are barred, and any GST/HST or PST component of taxable benefits eligible for input tax credits is deemed government assistance under subsection 248(16) and excluded. Under subsection 37(1.4) (enacted after LGL Ltd.), salaries or wages paid to employees performing SR&ED outside Canada qualify up to 10% of the claimant's directly attributable Canadian SR&ED salaries and wages.

For specified employees (subsection 248(1)—shareholders owning ≥10% of the shares of any class of the corporation or a related corporation, or individuals not dealing at arm's length with the employer), bonuses, profit-based remuneration, taxable benefits, and prior-year unpaid wages paid in the year are excluded (Regulation 2900(9)), and Regulation 2900(7) restricts the salary-base inclusion for each specified employee under the proxy method to the lesser of: (1) 75% of the specified employee's total eligible salary or wages (SR&ED and non-SR&ED combined) for the year, or (2) 2.5 × A × (B ÷ 365), where A is the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) under section 18 of the Canada Pension Plan for the calendar year in which the tax year ends, and B is the number of days in the tax year the claimant employed the individual (with no proration for days the employee was not a specified employee). Under Regulation 2900(8) and (10), if a specified employee is employed by associated corporations (including deemed associated related individuals or partnerships) in tax years ending in the same calendar year, the single 2.5 × YMPE cap must be shared across the associated group.
4.2 Subcontractors, Non-Arm's-Length Transfers, and Third-Party Payments

When an arm's-length taxable Canadian supplier performs SR&ED work in Canada on behalf of a claimant (subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01)), 100% of the eligible contract expense enters the section 37 deductible pool and 80% enters qualified expenditures for ITC purposes (Form T661, Line 529), provided the amount is paid within 180 days of year-end (Line 528 backs out unpaid non-salary current expenses) and complies with prepaid expense limits (subsection 18(9)). Claimants must maintain contracts, statements of work, and technical descriptions of the contractor's experimentation in Part 2 of Form T661. Contract R&D performed outside Canada earns 0% federal ITC.

Where SR&ED is subcontracted to a non-arm's-length party (section 37 and subsection 127(13)), direct contract payments are ineligible for ITCs in the payer's hands; instead, the related performer either claims its own underlying SR&ED costs or files Form T1146 jointly with the payer under subsection 127(13) to transfer qualified expenditures to the corporate payer. Separately, third-party payments (subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(i.1) and (ii)) made to CRA-approved universities, colleges, research institutes, approved associations, granting councils, or tax-exempt non-profit SR&ED corporations (paragraph 149(1)(j)) for SR&ED in Canada related to the claimant's business—where the institution controls the research, results are generally published, and the claimant holds a preferential right to exploit results—are 100% deductible in the section 37 pool and 80% eligible for federal ITCs (excluding building-related payments under subparagraph 37(8)(d)(iv)).
4.3 Materials Consumed vs. Materials Transformed

Under Regulation 2900(2)(a) (traditional method) and subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V) (proxy method), 100% of the cost of materials—purchased from either Canadian or foreign suppliers, including raw materials and direct pre-test processing costs such as galvanization—qualifies for both the section 37 pool and SR&ED ITCs when used directly in SR&ED in Canada as either materials consumed (rendered virtually valueless during testing) or materials transformed (integrated into an experimental prototype or pilot unit). Following Consoltex (97 DTC 724), subsections 127(27) to (36) impose ITC recapture if transformed materials or experimental prototypes are later sold or converted to commercial use (though Les Cultures Laflamme confirms subsequent sale of experimental output does not disqualify the underlying SR&ED labour). Conversely, general laboratory supplies—test tubes, pipettes, vials, beakers, flasks, filter papers, acids/solvents/soaps/lubricants not forming the experimental body, CDs/DVDs, cleaning supplies, and general facility utilities (water, electricity, natural gas, unless metered and proven directly consumed as an experimental process input)—are excluded from "materials for SR&ED" and treated strictly as overhead (claimable only under the traditional method).
4.4 Overhead Methodologies: Prescribed Proxy Amount (55%) vs. Traditional Method

In Part 3 of Form T661, claimants must elect annually between the Proxy Method (Line 160) and the Traditional Method (Line 162); the election is irrevocable for that taxation year once filed, and defaults to the Traditional Method if no box is ticked.

Under the Proxy Method (clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B) and Regulation 2900(4)), claimants avoid tracking indirect SR&ED overheads and instead compute a notional Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) in Part 5 (Line 820) equal to 55% of the directly engaged SR&ED salary base (subject to the Regulation 2900(7) specified employee limits and an overall business-deduction cap). (Audit Note: Outdated secondary blogs occasionally print a pre-2014 65% proxy formula; the statutory rate on Form T661 Line 820 is 55%.) Because the 55% PPA enters qualified expenditures on Line 502, every $1.00 of non-specified Canadian T4 SR&ED salary enters the ITC base at $1.55, generating 54.25% ($1.55 × 35%) in federal refundable ITCs alone for a qualifying CCPC or ECPC—nearly double the 28.00% ($0.80 × 35%) earned on arm's-length Canadian subcontractors. Neither the PPA nor actual overheads enter the section 37 SR&ED pool; actual overheads are deducted normally in computing business income.

Under the Traditional Method (clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A) and Regulation 2900(2)(c) and 2900(3)(b)), claimants must specifically identify, track, allocate, and substantiate every overhead and personnel expense (such as indirect SR&ED support wages, shop-floor utilities, lab glassware, and SR&ED employee relocation/hiring expenses) that is directly related and incremental to the prosecution of SR&ED. Qualifying traditional overheads enter both the section 37 pool and the ITC base, making the Traditional Method advantageous primarily for utility- or facility-heavy industrial trials with low internal payroll.
4.5 Cloud Computing, Software Subscriptions, and Data Infrastructure Costs

Under existing ITA rules, purchased software licences and acquired IP rights are non-eligible for SR&ED deductions and ITCs (though acquired software and computer hardware may qualify for accelerated CCA outside SR&ED under the Productivity Super-Deduction or proposed Mega Deduction). Cloud computing (e.g., AWS, Azure, GCP) and SaaS subscriptions are treated as overhead/service expenses rather than consumed materials: under the Proxy Method, they are subsumed within the 55% PPA and cannot be claimed separately, whereas under the Traditional Method, cloud compute subscriptions qualify only where proven directly related and incremental to SR&ED experiments (e.g., dedicated metered GPU instances segregated from commercial production). Crucially, however, Bill C-15's restoration of capital and lease expenditures means that dedicated physical GPU servers and Canadian compute hardware purchased (Line 390) or leased (Line 350) after December 15, 2024 and used ≥90% (ASA) in Canadian SR&ED (excluding general-purpose office computers) can now be claimed directly even when electing the 55% Proxy Method.
4.6 Restored Capital Expenditures, Lease Costs, Shared-Use Equipment, and ITC Recapture
Enacted Bill C-15 reinstated SR&ED tax incentives for capital property and equipment leases—previously excluded since January 1, 2014—subject to strict statutory parameters.

For All or Substantially All (ASA ≥90%) Capital Property (Form T661, Line 390), claimants may claim the full laid-down acquisition cost (purchase price, installation, customs/excise duties, and freight) of depreciable property acquired and becoming available for use after December 15, 2024, provided at acquisition the claimant intended either to use the property ≥90% of its operating time over its expected useful life to perform SR&ED in Canada or to consume ≥90% of its value in performing SR&ED in Canada. Similarly, ASA Equipment Lease Costs (Line 350) incurred / first payable after December 15, 2024 for equipment used ≥90% of operating time in Canadian SR&ED are fully restored as current SR&ED expenditures (earning 100% refundability at the 35% CCPC/ECPC rate). Conversely, non-depreciable land, buildings, and leasehold interests in buildings (subparagraph 37(8)(d)(ii)) are excluded; general-purpose office equipment or furniture (GPOP) is excluded under the Proxy Method; annual depreciation/amortization is excluded; and previously used depreciable property qualifies for immediate section 37 pool deduction on Line 390 but earns 0% SR&ED ITC.

Where new depreciable equipment (other than GPOP) acquired after December 15, 2024 falls below the 90% lifetime ASA threshold but is used primarily (>50%) in Canadian SR&ED, it qualifies as Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) (Line 504 & Part 6C) for ITC purposes only: the capital cost is depreciated via standard CCA on Schedule 8 rather than entering the section 37 pool, while earning SR&ED ITCs on 25% of capital cost in the first period (first-term SUE) and 25% in the second period (second-term SUE), up to 50% total. For qualifying CCPCs and ECPCs, enhanced 35% ITCs earned on capital expenditures (ASA or SUE) are 40% refundable (14% cash refund + 21% non-refundable carryforward), and any subsequent sale or conversion to commercial use of SR&ED capital property, SUE, or contract-acquired physical property triggers ITC recapture under subsection 127(27).

body.text: 5. Governing Authorities, Pre-Claim Approval, Tax Forms, and Statutory Deadlines
5.1 Institutional Roles of Finance Canada and the Canada Revenue Agency

Tax policy design and statutory drafting for federal SR&ED rest exclusively with the Department of Finance Canada, whereas claim administration, technical scientific evaluation, financial verification, and audit compliance are executed by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA). The CRA also administers provincial and territorial R&D tax credits on behalf of seven provinces and Yukon through the federal T2/T1 tax system, while Revenu Québec administers Québec's CRIC/IDCI financially (relying on federal SR&ED technical definitions/reviews) and Alberta Tax and Revenue Administration (TRA) administers Alberta's Innovation Employment Grant on the AT1 corporate return. CRA outreach services include monthly English and French Microsoft Teams webinars on general SR&ED rules and pre-claim approval, as well as one-on-one consultations (OESCPB-SVEDGPO@cra-arc.gc.ca), while legacy sector-specific guidelines for physicians and medical professional corporations have been formally archived.
5.2 The Optional CRA Pre-Claim Approval Process (Launched April 2026)

Implemented on April 1, 2026 as part of Budget 2025's mandate to provide upfront R&D certainty and halve claim processing times, the CRA's Pre-Claim Approval Process allows eligible businesses to obtain a formal technical eligibility determination before beginning R&D work or incurring major costs (or shortly after starting work). Participation is optional. Under official CRA eligibility rules (updated October 14, 2026), the applicant must be a CCPC, another Canadian corporation, or a partnership, have gross business income of less than $25,000,000, and be in good compliance standing with the CRA, while the proposed project must not have been included in any prior SR&ED claim and must not involve issues currently under litigation.
Applicants follow a three-step digital workflow:

items: Request a Case Number: Confirm business and project eligibility criteria and obtain a CRA pre-claim case number.
Complete the Application: Answer required technical project questions and assemble supporting project planning documentation.
Submit via My Business Account: Upload the completed package electronically through the CRA's My Business Account portal.

body.text: The CRA issues a pre-claim approval determination within 8 weeks. When subsequently filing Form T661, the claimant ticks Line 212 and enters the case number on Line 214, qualifying for a streamlined 90-day processing standard if the pre-approved claim is selected for post-filing expenditure review.
5.3 Prescribed Federal Forms and May 2026 Line-by-Line Reporting Updates

In May 2026, the CRA issued updated versions of all five core federal SR&ED forms (Form T661, T2 Schedule 31, T2 Schedule 49, Form T1145, and Form T1146) incorporating Bill C-15's statutory changes. Alongside strict word-count limits in Part 2 Section B technical narratives (Guide T4088)—and special off-form secure mailing procedures where a federal agency designates a project as "classified information" for national security reasons—claimants completing the May 15, 2026 version of Form T661 must verify exact reporting across the newly updated fields: Line 207 requires the five-digit Field of Research code (RDF#####) from page 18 of Statistics Canada's Canadian Research and Development Classification (CRDC) 2020 Version 2.0; Lines 212 and 214 record pre-claim approval status and case numbers; Lines 262 and 263 list the 10 most expensive post-December 15, 2024 capital properties per project and their project operating-time percentages; Line 350 captures post-December 15, 2024 ASA equipment lease costs; Line 390 and Boxes 782 and 786 report full laid-down capital cost and comma-separated project numbers (matching Line 750 in Part 6A) for ASA depreciable property; and Line 504 with Part 6C Boxes 788–796 itemizes the 20 most expensive Shared-Use Equipment assets (Box 788 name, Box 790 YYYY-MM-DD purchase date, Box 792 25% capital cost, Box 794 "1" for first-term or "2" for second-term SUE, and Box 796 project numbers).
5.4 The Absolute 18-Month Statutory Filing Bar and Claim Preparer Penalties

Under subsection 37(11) and paragraph 127(9)(m) of the ITA, a taxpayer cannot deduct SR&ED expenditures or earn SR&ED ITCs unless the prescribed forms (Form T661 plus T2 Schedule 31 for corporations or Form T2038(IND) for individuals/trusts) containing all prescribed information are filed on or before the SR&ED reporting deadline: 12 months after the taxpayer's income tax return filing-due date. For corporations, whose T2 return is due 6 months after tax year-end, the SR&ED deadline is 18 months after the end of the taxation year (though tax court commentary recommends filing by 15 months or alongside the timely 6-month T2 return to mitigate filing defects). For individuals and trusts (subsection 104(2) and paragraph 150(1)(c)), the deadline is 12 months after their respective T1 or T3 filing-due dates. For partnerships, where all members are corporations, Form T661 is due 12 months after the 5-month partnership information return deadline (17 months after fiscal period-end); where members combine individuals/trusts and corporations, the underlying return is due on the earlier of March 31 or 5 months after fiscal period-end (+ 12 months).

Crucially, subsection 220(2.2) prohibits the Minister of National Revenue from granting any discretionary extension to file SR&ED prescribed forms (overriding pre-2005 jurisprudence in Alex Parallel Computers). Once the 18-month bar passes, no new projects or substitute expenditures may be added to offset audit disallowances (subsection 37(12)), omitting Schedule 31 forfeits the entire ITC (Easyway Cattle Co., 2015 TCC 211), filing projects under a sibling corporation's return is fatal (Westsource, 2017 TCC 9), and mailed claims lacking proof of timely filing fail (Fooi, 2024, contrasted with Windsor, 2024, where clarifying timely filed data preserved appeal rights). Finally, subsections 162(5.1) to (5.3) impose a $1,000 penalty (subject to a due diligence defence under 162(5.2)) if complete SR&ED claim preparer and billing-arrangement disclosures are omitted or misstated on Form T661. (Budget 2026 also proposed general inflation adjustments doubling or tripling older ITA administrative penalties while leaving newer penalties largely unchanged.)

body.text: 6. Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit and IP Box Regimes

Ten of Canada's thirteen provinces and territories operate subnational R&D tax credits. Following Bill C-15's enactment in March 2026, subnational regimes split between full federal alignment (led by British Columbia), autonomous restructuring (led by Québec), and holdout caps (such as Ontario, Alberta, Manitoba, and Saskatchewan).
6.1 Québec: The CRIC Overhaul and the IDCI Patent Box Regime

Administered by Revenu Québec, Québec's March 25, 2025 Budget introduced the Tax Credit for R&D and Pre-Commercialization (Crédit d'impôt pour la recherche, l'innovation et la commercialisation — CRIC) for taxation years or fiscal periods beginning after March 25, 2025, simultaneously abolishing seven legacy measures: (1) the R&D researcher salary/wage credit (formerly 14%–30% with a $50,000–$225,000 asset-linked exclusion threshold); (2) the university/public research centre/consortium contract credit; (3) the research consortium fees/dues credit (with transitional fee-balance claims permitted for tax years ending on or before December 31, 2029); (4) the private partnership pre-competitive research credit; (5) the technological adaptation services credit; (6) the industrial design component of the design credits (fashion design remains eligible); and (7) the foreign researcher/expert personal tax holiday. (Legacy credits apply only to taxation years beginning before March 26, 2025.)

Available to all qualified corporations (CCPCs, public companies, and foreign-controlled subsidiaries) with a Québec establishment, CRIC is 100% refundable at 30% on up to $1,000,000 of eligible expenditures exceeding the exclusion threshold (shared among associated groups via Form RD-1029.8.EN-T, and subject to prior R&D claim / <$50 million financial-statement asset rules where applicable) and 20% on all excess eligible expenditures. The annual exclusion threshold equals the greater of $50,000 or the sum of the R&D employees threshold and pre-commercialization employees threshold (estimated by R&D tax advisors at $18,571 × % of eligible time per employee, with Revenu Québec refunds typically processed in 60–90 days according to advisory practice). Crucially, CRIC covers both R&D and pre-commercialization activities—regulatory certification testing, technological validations, studies, and product design (shape, aesthetics, functionality, materials)—that continue Québec R&D, applying to 100% of salaries, 100% of eligible capital property acquisitions (excluding tax-holiday large investment projects), and 50% of subcontracting costs (including certified public research centres, universities, and consortia), claimed on Form RD-1029.8.CR-T and RD-1029.8.PR-T. (Software firms in Québec also evaluate the separate e-business tax credit, CDAE, up to 30%.)

On the commercialization side, Québec's Incentive Deduction for the Commercialization of Innovations (IDCI) (L.Q. 2021, c. 14, ss. 76 and 198, claimed on Form CO-737.18.CI) reduces the Québec corporate tax rate from 11.5% to an effective 2.0% (a 17.0% combined federal-Québec rate vs. 26.5% standard) on qualified profits from patents, certificates of supplementary protection, copyrighted software, and plant breeders' rights developed substantially in Québec. Qualifying income covers royalties, embedded IP sales/leasing/service revenue, and infringement damages, excluding capital gains on IP transfers, trademarks, and trade secrets. Compliant with OECD BEPS Action 5, the deduction equals [(A × B ÷ C) − D] × (E ÷ F) × G, where A is net income for tax purposes, B ÷ C is the QIPA gross-revenue fraction, D is routine non-IP profit, E ÷ F is the cumulative 7-year moving-average Québec R&D nexus ratio, and G = (11.5% − 2.0%) ÷ 11.5% = 0.826087 (82.61%) (correcting a 0.826% typographical unit error on Québec's summary webpage). IDCI stacks cumulatively with SR&ED and CRIC, though CRIC pre-commercialization expenses are excluded from the IDCI nexus fraction.
6.2 Ontario: OITC, ORDTC, and OBRITC Three-Tier Architecture

Administered by the CRA under the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario), Ontario provides three corporate R&D credits for permanent establishments in the province. First, the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC) provides an 8% fully refundable credit on up to $3,000,000 of qualified current Ontario SR&ED expenditures (maximum $240,000/year), phasing out between $500,000 and $800,000 of prior-year federal taxable income OR $25,000,000 and $50,000,000 of prior-year specified/paid-up capital (Schedule 566 / T2SCH31; Ontario has not adopted the federal $6 million limit or confirmed capital expenditures in the OITC base). Second, the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC) provides an uncapped 3.5% non-refundable credit for all non-exempt corporations (3-year carryback, 20-year carryforward; recapture under section 45 at 23.56% on Schedule 508 / Schedule 5 Line 277), which—per official Ontario guidance—explicitly includes 100% of qualified capital expenditures made on or after December 16, 2024. Because ORDTC is reduced by OITC/OBRITC and itself reduces the federal 35% refundable SR&ED base as government assistance, pre-profit CCPCs routinely waive current-year ORDTC under subsection 43(1) of the Taxation Act, 2007. Third, the Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC, section 97) delivers a 20% fully refundable credit on up to $20,000,000 annually (maximum $4,000,000/year) for qualified Ontario R&D contracts with designated Eligible Research Institutes (Schedules 568 and 569).
6.3 Western Provinces: British Columbia's Permanent Aligned Credit, Alberta's IEG, Saskatchewan, and Manitoba

British Columbia (Income Tax Act [B.C.], sections 97–103, Form T666, strict 18-month deadline) fully aligned with Bill C-15 for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024—doubling its 10% refundable expenditure limit from $3 million to $6,000,000 (up to $600,000 cash), widening its taxable-capital phase-out to $15,000,000–$75,000,000, extending 10% refundability to ECPCs alongside CCPCs, restoring capital expenditures, and removing the credit's expiry date permanently in B.C. Budget 2026 (with a 10% non-refundable credit above $6 million or for other corporations; 3-year carryback / 10-year carryforward; non-refundable renunciation allowed; recapture applies).

Alberta (Alberta Corporate Tax Act, sections 26.95–26.99, administered by Alberta TRA on AT1 Schedule 29 and AT4970, due 15 months after the AT1 filing-due date) operates the fully refundable Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) on up to $4,000,000 of annual Alberta R&D spending (phased out across $10,000,000–$50,000,000 of prior-year Schedule 33 taxable capital via [($40,000,000 − (Taxable Capital − $10,000,000))] ÷ $40,000,000), paying 8% up to the corporation's two-year average base amount plus 12% (20% combined) on incremental spending above that two-year average; per June 2026 TRA guidance, Alberta retained its $4 million cap and pulls current federal SR&ED expenditures only (T661 Line 557), excluding restored capital costs.

Saskatchewan (The Income Tax Act [Saskatchewan], sections 63–63.4, T2SCH403) offers a 10% credit, doubling the CCPC 10% refundable tier from $1 million to the first $2,000,000 of qualifying expenditures incurred on or after December 16, 2024, with a 10% non-refundable credit (3-year carryback / 10-year carryforward; renunciation allowed) above $2 million or for non-CCPCs, capped at $1,000,000 in total annual credits. Manitoba (Income Tax Act [Manitoba], section 7.3, T2SCH380, due 12 months after filing-due date) provides an uncapped 15% credit covering current and provincial depreciable capital costs (excluding buildings): half (7.5%) is refundable and half non-refundable (3-year carryback / 20-year carryforward; federal renunciation within 6 months of year-end) for in-house R&D, while R&D under contract with qualifying Manitoba institutes is 100% refundable (full 15%).
6.4 Atlantic Provinces, Yukon, and Non-Participating Jurisdictions

Nova Scotia (section 41, T2SCH340, 18-month deadline post year-end; recapture applies; renunciation within 6 months of year-end), New Brunswick (section 59, T2SCH360; recapture applies), and Newfoundland and Labrador (section 42, T2SCH301 / Form T1129, 12 months after filing-due date; uniquely open to individuals/trusts/partnerships and unreduced by non-GST/HST assistance) each provide an uncapped 15% fully refundable R&D tax credit, while Yukon provides a 15% fully refundable credit plus 5% (20% total) on eligible payments to Yukon University. None of these four jurisdictions had announced adoption of the federal $6 million enhanced cap or new capital rules through late October 2026 (since their 15% refundable rates are already uncapped). Prince Edward Island, Northwest Territories, and Nunavut offer no territorial/provincial R&D tax credit, leaving federal SR&ED unreduced by provincial assistance (supplemented in PEI by direct Innovation PEI grants).

body.text: 7. Direct Federal R&D Grants, Government Assistance, and Credit Stacking Mechanics
7.1 Flagship Federal Innovation Grants: NRC IRAP, Strategic Innovation Fund, and Global Innovation Clusters

Canadian R&D performers routinely stack direct federal innovation grants with SR&ED tax credits. The National Research Council – Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP) supports incorporated, for-profit Canadian SMEs through technical advisory services delivered by Industrial Technology Advisors (ITAs) and non-repayable project contributions: funding directories note IRAP covers up to 75% of eligible project costs (with individual contributions reaching up to $10 million), while academic policy evaluation by John Lester (University of Calgary School of Public Policy) shows IRAP disbursements rose from ~$170 million/year (2012–2017) to $470 million in FY 2022–23 across roughly 2,900 projects annually, averaging 36.6% of approved project costs. (Although Ottawa announced in December 2023 that NRC IRAP would integrate into a new Canada Innovation Corporation [CIC] by 2026–27, Budget 2026 continued allocating renewed clean-tech support and $75 million over three years for IP Assist directly to the NRC.) Unlike retrospective SR&ED claims, IRAP requires an approved contribution agreement prior to incurring project expenses. For larger-scale R&D and industrial transformation, Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada (ISED) administers the Strategic Innovation Fund (SIF) (reinforced in Budget 2025, alongside Budget 2026's $1 billion Strategic Response Fund investment for large-scale R&D and the Canada Strong Diversification Fund for tariff-affected manufacturers), Global Innovation Clusters (GICs) for collaborative multi-party IP projects, and Pan-Canadian AI compute infrastructure programs.
7.2 Statutory Government Assistance Grind and Optimal Credit Stacking Computations

Under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsections 127(9) and 127(18)–(20), all provincial R&D tax credits and direct grants (including IRAP, GICs, and concessional R&D loans per CAE Inc.) constitute government assistance that reduces the federal SR&ED expenditure base before the 35% or 15% federal ITC is calculated. Thus, a 15% provincial credit plus a 35% federal credit yields 44.75% of the qualified expenditure base (15% + [35% × 85%]), not 50%. Crucially, however, under the 55% Proxy Method, the 55% PPA in Part 5 of Form T661 is computed on 100% of directly engaged Canadian T4 SR&ED salaries before grants or provincial credits are deducted in Part 4 (and any subsequent repayment of government assistance is added back on Line 560). Consequently, an academic study of IRAP + SR&ED estimates an average combined effective subsidy rate of 64.9%, and practitioner calculators show typical all-in cash recovery of 60% to 70%+ of direct Canadian R&D payroll:

body.text: 8. Judicial Precedents, CRA Audit Standards, and Tax Controversy
8.1 The Foundational Five-Part Test and Appellate Doctrine

Canadian SR&ED eligibility is governed by the five-question test articulated in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen (97-531-IT-G, 1998 TCC) and affirmed by the Federal Court of Appeal in CW Agencies Inc. and National R&D Inc. v. Canada (2022 FCA 72):

items: Technological Risk or Uncertainty: Was there a scientific or technological uncertainty unresolvable by routine engineering or standard practice—including "system uncertainty" arising from integrating known components?
Hypotheses: Did qualified personnel formulate specific, scientifically grounded hypotheses aimed at reducing or eliminating that uncertainty (Novalia, 2016 TCC 81)?

Systematic Investigation: Did the methodology follow the scientific method—testing hypotheses by experiment or rigorous engineering/mathematical analysis (Hun-Medipharma, 1997 TCC) and observing measurable variables—rather than trial-and-error?
Technological Advancement: Did the process yield a technological advancement—including proving a plausible hypothesis false (Rainbow Pipe Line, 1999 TCC)?

Contemporaneous Documentation: Were detailed records of hypotheses, tests, and results kept as the work progressed (RIS-Christie, [1999] 1 C.T.C. 132 FCA; supplemented only in exceptional cases by highly credible oral testimony, Les Abeilles, 2014 TCC 313)?

body.text: 8.2 Contemporary Software, Systems Integration, and Engineering Jurisprudence (2023–2026)

Recent Tax Court rulings from 2023 through 2026 delineate where complex engineering qualifies and where commercial development fails. In Willowglen Systems Inc. v. The King (2026 TCC 7), the Tax Court split two industrial-software projects: it allowed the MTCLM SIL 4 train-control project based on cumulative system uncertainty unresolvable by standard methods, but disallowed $1,293,692 on the SCADACOM-5 SCADA upgrade, holding that modernizing and scaling software with known tools is product development rather than SR&ED. In Dazzm Inc. v. The King (2024 TCC 129), resolving systemic performance bottlenecks in React/Redux SaaS integration succeeded because metrics and developer testimony proved uncertainty beyond routine debugging, echoing hardware integration wins in Buhler (2023 TCC 18) and physician-MPC attribution in André Lamy MPC (2020 TCC 61), as well as international R&D tax treatment in BlackBerry Canada (2025, holding foreign R&D services income was not passive FAPI). Conversely, Vortex Energy Services Ltd. (2025 TCC 63), Tuna Temple Inc. (2025 TCC 183), and Paveit Construction Inc. (2025) rejected trial-and-error prototyping and evenly split batch wage estimates, whereas Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. (2025) succeeded by testing microbial stability hypotheses via logged pH and microbial counts.
8.3 Audit Defence, Statute-Barred Reassessments, Gross Negligence Penalties, and Dispute Resolution

Disputed CRA SR&ED reviews proceed from administrative review resolution to formal objection and, if unresolved, to the Tax Court of Canada via a Notice of Appeal setting out the assessment under appeal, material facts, statutory provisions, issues, and relief sought. Canada has no formal domestic tax mediation or arbitration (ADR); Ministerial discretion to cancel interest or penalties is restricted to extraordinary circumstances within a 10-year window, alongside Financial Administration Act remission orders and the CRA's Voluntary Disclosures Program (overhauled effective October 1, 2025). Crucially, in Les Éléments Chauffants Tempora Inc. v. The King (2025 TCC 173), although some 2007–2008 heating-element projects qualified technically, the Tax Court held that copying supplier/manufacturer website text into SR&ED technical narratives constituted negligent misrepresentation—reopening statute-barred years nearly a decade later, upholding gross negligence penalties (subsection 163(2)), and exposing shareholders to personal derivative assessments (section 160), reinforcing prior fraud-fine precedents of 150%–300% (R. v. Elhami, 2017 QCCQ 2684; Tempora, SCC 2018) and broad waiver-reassessment exposure (Rio Tinto Alcan, 2017 TCC 67).

cells: Taxpayer Win (4 of 5 projects) — Established the 5-part test (uncertainty, hypotheses, scientific method, advancement, contemporaneous records) and "system uncertainty".
Crown Win (Round 1) — A new product or patent alone does not prove SR&ED; contemporaneous testing records are essential.
Taxpayer Win — Conclusive rejection of a scientifically grounded hypothesis is itself a technological advancement.
Split Doctrine — Fixed-price commercial risk contracts do not grind SR&ED (Com Dev), whereas government R&D loans constitute assistance (CAE).
Crown Wins — Omitting Schedule 31 or filing projects under a related corporation's return forfeits credits past 18 months.
Taxpayer Win — Wages specifically structured to compensate solely SR&ED duties were 100% allowed without arbitrary time proration.
National R&D Inc. v. Canada, 2020 TCC 47, aff'd 2022 FCA 72
Crown Win — Accepted hypotheses alone are insufficient where remaining Northwest Hydraulic criteria are unproven.
Taxpayer Win — Systemic uncertainty in React/Redux open-source integration exceeded routine debugging when backed by metrics.
Split (2006/2009 Crown Win) — Plagiarized supplier website text in SR&ED reports reopened statute-barred years and upheld penalties.
Crown Wins — Reconstructed narratives, trial-and-error prototyping, and evenly split batch wage estimates fail SR&ED audits.
Willowglen Systems Inc. v. The King, 2026 TCC 7
Split Decision — Allowed SIL 4 train-control project on cumulative system uncertainty; disallowed $1,293,692 SCADA upgrade as routine scaling.
